newsitem.title: FINLAND: FEATURE - Modern Helsinki site reflects U.S. summit hopes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Modern Helsinki site reflects U.S. summit hopes.

text.p: Preparing for a summit to lay the ground for "a new security architecture for Europe", U.S. President Bill Clinton's staff seem to have been very careful in their choice of building.

The Americans, official hosts of the March 20 meeting -- in Helsinki so Russian President Boris Yeltsin can attend despite poor health -- were keen to find a site that would be free of associations with past Cold War encounters or previous presidents.
They chose Mantyniemi (pronounced Mantuniemi), the official residence of the President of Finland, built in 1993.

Nestling on a small promontory jutting out into the Baltic, among pine trees and wooden villas in parkland just outside the city centre, it is a prime example of modern Finnish architecture in a peaceful spot. The name means 'Pine Point'.

The modern, neutral focus is deliberate: top of the agenda is a U.S.-led bid to woo Russia into accepting expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) -- the former Warsaw Pact's greatest foe -- to include former east bloc states.
U.S. diplomats hope to overwrite the superpower polarisation of the Cold War years and bring the Russians over to a new way of thinking.
They are trying to convince them that NATO expansion is not a threat, but a natural development which reflects the realities of the post-Cold War period.

Helsinki suited both sides as a venue because Russia's western neighbour, militarily neutral during the Cold War and now a member of the European Union, appears to have no major axe to grind in the debate.
"It does help that Finland is outside NATO," said George Maude, a Finnish-based historian. The Finns "provide a less charged atmosphere for the meeting -- it is less one-sided".
However, given Finland's past, it was not as easy to find a venue to embody this new era in Helsinki, host to several major Cold War East-West encounters and home to just 700,000 people.
HISTORY LIMITS THE OPTIONS
Where else in the capital could they go?

The so-called "SALT Room" in the U.S. Embassy -- venue of the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty signings in the early 1970s -- was out. Hardly neutral ground, and in any case too small for a 90s summit.
The seaside hotel Kalastajatorppa, traditionally a guest house for visiting heads of state, is becoming somewhat faded and is already saturated with Cold War history.
Meetings there included the 1975 reception attended by 35 Soviet, U.S., East and West European leaders to adopt the Helsinki Final Act.
That occasion was a landmark in European security, setting up the Conference for Security and Co-operation in Europe (CSCE).
The Soviet Union and its communist allies won confirmation of post-World War Two borders, but in return provided commitments on human rights which later undermined their regimes in the late 1980s.

Given Russian political sensitivities, it may not be too diplomatic to bring Yeltsin to talks where Brezhnev toasted what former U.S. President Gerald Ford was later to call "a Trojan Horse for Liberty behind the Iron Curtain".
The presidential Palace, an imposing 19th-century mansion rebuilt by architect Carl Ludvig Engel -- creator of central Helsinki's neo-classical look -- was potentially a better option.
But it was often host to the tsars, and its stately ballrooms and galleries have also done much Cold War service.
Former U.S. president George Bush and Soviet reformer Mikhail Gorbachev were photographed among its chandeliers and classical paintings in 1990, a year before the USSR collapsed.
So this year, the building where Clinton and Yeltsin will get down to business will have no such associations.

A modern, airy, south-facing villa, Mantyniemi's mainly white interior spurns heavy forms and hard right-angles: sculptured in stone, wood and glass, its high ceilings and picture windows suggest the house is flooded in daylight.

If any interior can be conducive to calm discussion and lofty thoughts, this would be one. Sitting on elegant green chairs among glass sculptures and fresh, light-wooden floors feels almost like visiting a highly tasteful modern art gallery.
HELSINKI'S ROLE

Finland is now helping to set a soothing scene for the Russian leader to try to come to terms with a highly controversial strategic proposal by a former enemy, but officials stress that is the extent of its involvement.
The choice of Helsinki as a venue this time is rooted in geographical convenience; Finland is offering nearby facilities for a man recovering from illness.

An initiative of President Martti Ahtisaari, the idea came to him when he heard U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright say on television that the summit, originally due to take place in the United States, could be held elsewhere.
Helsinki's highly efficient and lavishly equipped hospitals -- which already treat those patients from Russia who have the money to pay -- will be on full alert.
Its advanced technology is also well capable of supporting modern media: up to 3,000 journalists are expected, with armies of television crews needing cable and satellite connections.

As an illustration of how technologically advanced Finland is, Web surfers with a good browser can inspect pictures of the summit venue and read the latest on the agenda from page www.vn.fi/vn/um/finfo/english/summit.html.
MEMORIES IN STONE

But even though the U.S. is emphasising progress and modernity in this summit, the capital of the former Grand Duchy of Russia, which went to war twice with its neighbour, still holds echoes of past Cold War darkness.

In the town centre is the Hotel Torni, headquarters of the Soviet-manned Allied Control Commission imposed on Finland after World War Two. Comfortable and quite luxurious today, its dark, heavy corridors still convey an air of mystery, even oppression.

Older Finns remember that the only constant enemy in their country's 80-year history has been their eastern neighbour, and note that while Russia may now be weak, it could again become belligerent and acquisitive.
In this context there is one feature of the president's beautiful Mantyniemi residence which, for the Finns at least, is a lasting symbol of the need for security.

"The building is...created on Finland's Cambrian Rock, which that great designer the Ice Age has wrought into a splendid structure," wrote Mantyniemi's main designer Reima Pietila. "The building is part of this landscape."
Rock -- granite -- is more prominent in Helsinki than soil. In Cold War days the people of the city viewed the granite as a godsend, because it meant protection against nuclear attack.
